entries.title: Project overview and headline figures
entries.content: Dashboard Royale analyses The Gilded Ace, a fictional 300-machine casino, for January–June 2025 using synthetic data (data release 0.9.0-draft). Tracked casino net $15,585,460.60; tracked wagering $163,804,869.65; tracked payouts $148,219,409.05. Property coin-in $248,905,219.25, house win $23,638,155.10, theoretical win $23,545,364.48. 1,226 operations tickets (1,207 fault repairs), 5,021.08 downtime hours. Comp cost $190,669.30 (face value $682,749.50). 82 of 82 verification checks pass.

entries.title: Q1: Which machines are underperforming?
entries.content: Q1 asks which machines underperform. The exposure-adjusted ranking compares each machine with same-configuration peers. It produced 10 preliminary candidates (not replacement orders): M-1014, M-1008, M-1045, M-1040, M-1230, M-1048, M-1265, M-1221, M-1227, M-1082. 10 of 10 are in the Back Forty zone. Back Forty earns $11.71 theoretical win per available machine hour versus $19.01 elsewhere, at 25.4% occupancy versus 38.5%. Conclusion: location, not the machines themselves, is the leading explanation.

entries.title: Q2: How did floor demand change?
entries.content: Q2 asks how floor demand changed. Monthly floor coin-in fluctuated rather than declining steadily: Jan $41.68M, Feb $39.58M, Mar $43.65M, Apr $41.29M, May $42.98M, Jun $39.73M. The highest month was Mar and the lowest Feb; January to June changed -4.7%. Change in daily coin-in per zone, January to June: Back Forty -10.1%; Bar Row -5.6%; Main Entrance -0.7%; Garage Entrance -5.9%; High-Limit Room -11.2%; Hotel Corridor -5.9%; Center Pit +10.5%. Daily foot traffic and coin-in are strongly correlated in Back Forty (r = 0.979), which is association, not proof that traffic causes play.

entries.title: Q3: How much play was lost to downtime?
entries.content: Q3 covers maintenance and downtime. There were 1,226 operations tickets, of which 1,207 were fault repairs; the others were installs, moves, scheduled maintenance and retirements. Total downtime was 5,021.08 hours (4,934.08 hours from fault repairs). An average fault repair waited 1.14 hours for a technician and took 2.95 hours to repair. Direct fault repair cost was $212,945.21. Estimated theoretical-win exposure from fault downtime was $88,346.72 — an upper-bound estimate, not actual lost revenue, because players can move to other machines. By manufacturer: Ridgeline 7.23 fault repairs per machine (680 repairs, 2,747 downtime hours, 94 machines); Northwind 3.02 fault repairs per machine (305 repairs, 1,288 downtime hours, 101 machines); Halcyon 1.93 fault repairs per machine (222 repairs, 899 downtime hours, 115 machines).

entries.title: Q4: What did tracked players wager, get back and net?
entries.content: Q4 covers tracked (loyalty-card) players, January–June. 113,890 players wagered $163,804,869.65 and were paid $148,219,409.05, a casino net of $15,585,460.60 (theoretical win $15,485,020.98). 80,992 players lost, 15,504 won and 17,394 broke even. Gross losses were $20,939,424.55 and winnings paid $5,353,963.95. Losses are concentrated: the top 1% of losing players account for 15.73% of gross losses, the top 5% for 40.73%, the top 10% for 52.84% and the top 20% for 66.52%. Gini coefficient of wagering 0.7536; of losses 0.6237.

entries.title: Q5: What did comps cost, and did anything change?
entries.content: Q5 covers the loyalty comp program. Actual economic comp cost was $190,669.30 against a face value of $682,749.50 (cost is 27.9% of face value), from 59,361 redemptions. From May 1 the points charged per comp dollar roughly halved in every tier (average points per face dollar, Jan–Apr to May–Jun: Base 15.0 to 7.0; Gold 12.0 to 5.6; Platinum 9.0 to 4.2). Average monthly comp cost rose from $30,812.60 (Jan–Apr) to $33,709.45 (May–Jun). Comp cost as a share of tracked theoretical win went from 1.11% in January to 1.32% in June. The data does not show whether the change was deliberate or whether it brought extra visits.

entries.title: Q6: Which actions would we fund with $100,000?
entries.content: Q6 asks which actions to fund with $100,000 for the 30 days from July 1, 2025. The challenge allows up to 3 action types from the action catalogue; keeping money (A-HOLD, $0 unit cost) does not use a slot. The plan: A-TECH-SHIFT (Add one technician to a shift for 30 days) quantity 1 at $11,520 each = $11,520, lead time 7 days, 23 days of effect; A-INSPECT (Machine inspection and paytable verification) quantity 10 at $1,200 each = $12,000, lead time 1 days, 29 days of effect; A-COMP-PILOT (Comp policy pilot with control group) quantity 1 at $4,000 each = $4,000, lead time 5 days, 25 days of effect. Total invested $27,520; preserved (A-HOLD) $72,480. All quantities are within catalogue limits, and only A-COMP-PILOT uses an incompatibility group (comp_policy).

entries.title: Q6: Why these actions were chosen
entries.content: A-TECH-SHIFT adds one technician to a shift for 30 days to test whether more repair staffing cuts response time and downtime (1,226 operations tickets, 1,207 fault repairs, 5,021.08 downtime hours). Waiting for a technician is 27.9% of fault downtime, so even eliminating it would recover at most about $4,089 of estimated exposure per 30 days, less than its cost: it is a measured test, not an investment expected to pay back. A-INSPECT checks the 10 Q1 candidates (10 in Back Forty) for faults and paytable issues before any costly relocation or replacement; the outcome is information, not a guaranteed finding. A-COMP-PILOT tests comp redemption pricing (which halved from May 1, see Q5) against a randomised control group. The remaining $72,480 is held until evidence supports more spending.

entries.title: Q6: How we would know the actions worked
entries.content: Each action is evaluated over the 30-day horizon against a January–June baseline and a comparison group. A-TECH-SHIFT: average response time, repair duration and fault downtime hours on the staffed shift versus the same shift in the Jan–Jun baseline and versus unchanged shifts. A-INSPECT: number of faults and paytable issues found and corrected, then availability versus uninspected Back Forty machines. A-COMP-PILOT: incremental net revenue (theoretical win minus comp cost) and repeat visits per player, treatment versus a randomised control group stratified by tier. A-HOLD: funds released only when a test supports another investment. Qualifications: downtime hours are not automatically lost revenue; fluctuating coin-in does not prove a comp change will raise it; these are hypotheses to test, not guaranteed outcomes.

entries.title: Q6: Actions considered but not funded
entries.content: Considered but not funded: A-REPLACE-BUY (Replace a machine with a purchased new title, $220,000); A-REPLACE-LEASE (Replace a machine with a leased new title, $33,800); A-WAYFINDING (Wayfinding and signage refresh for a zone, $7,500); A-PREVENTIVE (Preventive maintenance sweep for one manufacturer, $9,000); A-COMP-CHANGE (Change comp redemption rate floor-wide, $1,500); A-PROMO (Property promotion weekend, $15,000). Replacing machines exceeds the budget or would put new titles in the same low-traffic location; only 3 action types are allowed; a promotion's benefit is not established causally; a floor-wide comp change is mutually exclusive with the pilot and cannot separate the pricing effect from seasonality.

entries.title: Forecast model of daily coin-in
entries.content: A daily coin-in forecast was trained on 2025-01-01 to 2025-04-30 and tested on 2025-05-01 to 2025-06-30. Holdout error: Baseline 1 — training mean: MAE $218,258; Baseline 2 — weekday average: MAE $68,699; Weekday avg + AR(1) residual: MAE $68,624; Calendar regression (weekday + holiday + known events + trend): MAE $65,187. The calendar regression improves on the weekday average by $3,511 MAE, but the 95% confidence interval ($-4,530 to $16,591) includes zero, so the gain is not statistically conclusive. It is used for scheduling and as a measurement baseline, not to justify spending.

entries.title: Verified claim: The ten preliminary underperformers are all in Back Forty.
entries.content: Claim: The ten preliminary underperformers are all in Back Forty. Evidence used: prepared_daily_view → finalize_bottom_10 scoring (src/lib/q1.ts). Result: 10/10 in Z-B40; list reproduced exactly. Alternative explanation considered: The machines themselves are weak titles. Limitation: Score compares within config, not zone.

entries.title: Verified claim: Low earnings of the candidates are not explained by bad luck.
entries.content: Claim: Low earnings of the candidates are not explained by bad luck. Evidence used: Σ luck_residual_usd per machine. Result: 9 of 10 earned ≥ theo over Jan–Jun. Alternative explanation considered: High-volatility variance. Limitation: Six months is short for high-volatility games.

entries.title: Verified claim: Back Forty demand fell with its foot traffic.
entries.content: Claim: Back Forty demand fell with its foot traffic. Evidence used: zone_month + zone_traffic_hourly. Result: Coin-in/day −10.1%, entries/hr −10.3% Jan→Jun; daily r = 0.979. Alternative explanation considered: Seasonality or citywide visitor decline. Limitation: Entries ≠ visitors; correlation shares weekly cycle.

entries.title: Verified claim: Ridgeline machines are the main source of downtime.
entries.content: Claim: Ridgeline machines are the main source of downtime. Evidence used: operations ⋈ machines, fault repairs per machine. Result: 7.23 repairs/machine vs 3.02 and 1.93. Alternative explanation considered: Ridgeline machines are older or busier. Limitation: Age and usage not controlled.

entries.title: Verified claim: Fault downtime exposed ≈ $88k of theo over six months.
entries.content: Claim: Fault downtime exposed ≈ $88k of theo over six months. Evidence used: downtime × machine theo/available hr. Result: $88,346.72 (estimate). Alternative explanation considered: Players switch to other machines. Limitation: Upper bound; not actual lost revenue.

entries.title: Verified claim: An extra technician cannot pay back in 30 days.
entries.content: Claim: An extra technician cannot pay back in 30 days. Evidence used: response share of fault downtime. Result: 27.9% → ≤ $4,089 exposure / 30 days < $11,520. Alternative explanation considered: Faster response shortens repair too. Limitation: Ignores staff-coverage side benefits.

entries.title: Verified claim: Tracked casino net was $15,585,460.60.
entries.content: Claim: Tracked casino net was $15,585,460.60. Evidence used: Σ coin-in − Σ payout, player_period. Result: Matches; reconciles to gross losses − winnings. Alternative explanation considered: —. Limitation: Carded play only.

entries.title: Verified claim: Losses are highly concentrated.
entries.content: Claim: Losses are highly concentrated. Evidence used: ranked per-player casino net. Result: Top 5% of losers = 40.73% of gross losses. Alternative explanation considered: A few lucky/unlucky sessions. Limitation: Within-period netting.

entries.title: Verified claim: Comp cost reconciles across three sources.
entries.content: Claim: Comp cost reconciles across three sources. Evidence used: player_period vs property_day vs loyalty_ledger. Result: $190,669.30 / $682,749.50 in all three. Alternative explanation considered: —. Limitation: Comp cost already inside F&B COGS.

entries.title: Verified claim: Points charged per comp dollar halved on May 1.
entries.content: Claim: Points charged per comp dollar halved on May 1. Evidence used: ledger redeems by gaming day, tier, benefit. Result: Base 15.0→7.0, Gold 12.0→5.6, Platinum 9.0→4.2. Alternative explanation considered: Tier mix shift (ruled out: every tier halved). Limitation: No policy record; cause not attributed.

entries.title: Verified claim: A calendar model forecasts coin-in slightly better than a weekday average.
entries.content: Claim: A calendar model forecasts coin-in slightly better than a weekday average. Evidence used: Jan–Apr train, May–Jun holdout. Result: MAE $65,187 vs $68,699; CI includes 0. Alternative explanation considered: Holdout noise. Limitation: Not statistically conclusive.
